Questions: What is the Sunset Park Sun, and how did 78 neighbors help create it?
Story Headline (If published): Welcome to the Sunset Park Sun!
Story Description or Prompt: The first issue's opening note introduced the bulletin as a monthly publication made by Sunset Park residents, journalists, and librarians, and credited the 78 neighbors who shaped it across ten community meetings at the library since October. It laid out what the team hoped readers would see in it: a way to follow curiosity into questions and action, to build trust between neighbors, and to take pride in the neighborhood.

Questions: When will the Sunset Park Recreation Center reopen, and how can you track a city construction project?
Story Description or Prompt: Working group member Judith C. tracked down a definitive answer from NYC Parks that construction on the Sunset Park Recreation Center would finish in October 2025, revised from the earlier March projection. The story ran with a companion breakdown of the tools she used to get it — the NYC Capital Project Tracker, 311, Community Board 7, and the Parks Department — as a model for how residents can get answers out of the city.

Questions: What is the Library Newsroom Field Guide, and where can it take you in Sunset Park?
Story Headline (If published): Explore Sunset Park with the Library Newsroom Field Guide
Story Description or Prompt: The team introduced the Library Newsroom Field Guide, a free printed booklet of prompts meant to get neighbors exploring Sunset Park and talking to the people in it. Resident Susan Parker described using it to reach Bush Terminal Park, the Army Terminal ferry, and her first Community Board 7 meeting.

Questions: What do you need to know before voting in the June 24 primary?
Story Headline (If published): There’s a Primary Election on June 24. Are You Voting?
Story Description or Prompt: A guide to the June 24 citywide primary explained what a primary is, why the local offices on the ballot matter, and what voters needed to do before election day. It listed the key dates — June 14 registration deadline, early voting June 14 to 22, primary day June 24, and the November 4 general — and pointed readers to a QR-coded rundown of every office and candidate.

Questions: How does ranked choice voting work in New York City elections?
Story Headline (If published): What you need to know about Ranked Choice Voting
Story Description or Prompt: Ahdya A. walked readers through how ranked choice voting works in the city races that use it: mayor, comptroller, public advocate, city council, and borough president. The piece covered the three rules voters most needed — you may rank up to five candidates, you are not required to rank five, and ranking the same candidate twice only counts your first choice.

Questions: What are Sunset Park's new residential trash rules, and when do official city bins arrive?
Story Headline (If published): Got Questions About the New Trash Rules?
Story Description or Prompt: Rebecca McCray summarized the residential trash rules that took effect November 12, 2024, requiring buildings with one to nine units to use secure-lidded bins of 55 gallons or smaller, set out after 6 p.m. on collection day. She listed the fine schedule, the most common violations, and the June 2026 switch to required official city bins.

Questions: How does composting work in Sunset Park, and where can you drop off food scraps?
Story Description or Prompt: Becca Elzinga explained the composting rules that took effect April 1, requiring residents to separate food scraps, yard waste, and food-soiled paper into a DSNY brown bin or a labeled bin of their own. She laid out the alternatives to curbside pickup — orange Smart Bins, green public bins, and three local drop-off sites — and noted that curbside and Smart Bin scraps go to anaerobic codigestion rather than becoming soil.

Questions: What's Behind the Menu at L'Wren?
Story Headline (If published): What’s Behind the Menu… at L’Wren?
Story Description or Prompt: Maureen C. and Carmen R. profiled L'wren, the 5th Avenue bar and restaurant that Travis and Jessica Klaus opened in a former furniture store in 2018. The piece traced its shift from a popcorn-only bar to a Latin-Asian fusion menu after the pandemic, and covered the happy hour, the back events room, and the couple's two-year search for the right location.

Questions: What happened after the first Sunset Park Sun went out?
Story Headline (If published): While you're reading the big headlines, here are the neighborhood ones
Story Description or Prompt: The second issue's opening note thanked neighbors for the response to the first, noting that 300 copies were printed and the stack at the library disappeared within hours. The team framed the bulletin as a space for Sunset Park amid a noisy wider world, and invited readers to send back ideas, questions, and connections.

Questions: Think you might be a victim of wage theft? Where can you learn your rights in Sunset Park?
Story Headline (If published): Think You Might Be a Victim of Wage Theft? Come to a Free Session at the Library July 19
Story Description or Prompt: The team previewed a free July 19 wage theft session at the Sunset Park Library, hosted with Documented, a nonprofit news organization covering immigrants in New York City. Labor experts and lawyers were set to walk through common examples of wage theft and how to look up an employer on Documented's Wage Theft Monitor, with sessions in Spanish at 12:30 p.m. and Chinese at 2 p.m.

Questions: What has the Sunset Park Library meant to one neighbor across six decades?
Story Headline (If published): Where the Stories Began: A Memory of Sunset Park Library
Story Description or Prompt: Diana M. recounted her first visit to the Sunset Park Library in the 1960s, when it was still called South Branch and her older brother William left her there for an afternoon that turned into a lifelong love of reading. She traced the branch through its 1970 closure and 1972 rebuild to the 2023 renovation, and reflected on what stayed the same even as the buildings changed.

Questions: What happened in the June 24 primary, and who's heading to the general election?
Story Headline (If published): There Was a 2025 Primary Election on June 24. Here’s What Happened
Story Description or Prompt: Ahdya A. and Terry Parris Jr. reported the early results of the June 24 citywide primary, led by Andrew Cuomo's concession and Zohran Mamdani's win of the Democratic nomination for mayor. The piece listed the general election field and the Democratic and Republican primary winners in races representing Sunset Park, along with early voting dates and the November 4 election day.

Questions: Where can Sunset Park residents find immigration resources and legal help?
Story Headline (If published): Looking for Immigrant Resources in Sunset Park? Here’s a Short List
Story Description or Prompt: Ray A. compiled a starting list of immigration resources available to Sunset Park residents, including Mixteca, South Brooklyn Mutual Aid, Brooklyn Defenders, Make the Road New York, and the New York Immigration Coalition. The piece described what each organization offers, noted the list was not exhaustive, and pointed to QR codes linking to addresses in English, Spanish, and Chinese.

Questions: What's Behind the Menu at Cafe Nube?
Story Headline (If published): What’s Behind the Menu at... Cafe Nube?
Story Description or Prompt: Maureen C. and Carmen R. profiled Cafe Nube, the part cafe, part art gallery that brothers Allen and Ron Lee opened near the 36th Street subway station in December 2019 with their parents. The story covered the small menu built to cut waste, the decision to raise prices only twice since opening, and the rotating gallery shows the brothers now curate themselves.

Questions: What is the most common hawk soaring over Sunset Park?
Story Headline (If published): Sunset Park Bird of the Month: The Red-Tailed Hawk
Story Description or Prompt: Charlie DeWitt launched a Bird of the Month feature with the red-tailed hawk, the bird he sees most often in the park and in Green-Wood Cemetery. The piece described the hawk's hunting, nesting, and mating habits, and asked readers to write in when they spot one overhead.

Questions: What does a 1979 documentary reveal about Sunset Park?
Story Headline (If published): Come Watch a 1979 Documentary About Sunset Park on July 8 at the Library
Story Description or Prompt: The team previewed a July 8 screening at the Sunset Park Library of Sunset Park, a 17-minute 1979 documentary produced by The Anchor Savings Bank and co-sponsored by Community Board 7, the Pratt Center, and the Sunset Park Restoration Committee. The piece sketched the Restoration Committee's history of house tours, curriculum work, and local housing research, and invited attendees to stay for a conversation afterward.

Questions: Where does Sunset Park begin and end — and who decides?
Story Headline (If published): How a Simple Map of Sunset Park Sparked a Question - and then a Story
Story Description or Prompt: Terry Parris Jr. opened the third issue by returning to the October 2024 kickoff session, where about 25 neighbors marked the places that mattered to them on a map of Sunset Park and started asking where its borders actually were. The note reported that no single answer emerged — people described their edges through daily routine, and the only line everyone agreed on was the water to the west — and framed the rest of the issue as a tour of the neighborhood's nooks.

Questions: Why can't anyone agree on Sunset Park's borders?
Story Headline (If published): Where Does Sunset Park Start and Stop? Not All the Maps Match.
Story Description or Prompt: Michal N. compared how Google Maps, the New York Times' 2023 crowd-sourced neighborhood map, and Community Board 7 each draw Sunset Park's boundaries, and found that no two matched. She also collected building names that point somewhere else — Park Slope Homes on 41st Street, two Linden Heights sites, Sunset Ridge Cafe, the former Bay Ridge Savings Bank on 5th Avenue, and a Greenwood Heights Reformed Church property marker — and asked who gets to decide what a neighborhood is called.

Questions: What neighborhood history lives in your family's closet?
Story Headline (If published): History Lives in Our Homes, Not Just in Our Museums
Story Description or Prompt: Ciel J. P. wrote about how neighborhood history survives in family closets rather than institutions, using the NYC Municipal Archives' 722,485 tax photos from 1939–41 and the 1940s.nyc map built from them. She sat with her grandmother Altagracia and great aunt Delfina to find a demolished family home at 5212 6th Avenue, and used the piece to announce the Sunset Park Museum initiative and a call for residents' own photographs.

Questions: What's Behind the Menu at Sole Cafe?
Story Headline (If published): What's Behind the Menu at... Sole Cafe?
Story Description or Prompt: Maureen C. and Carmen R. profiled Sole Cafe, the small shop at 5th Avenue and 34th Street that Daniel Mentado and Melissa Wen opened in 2025 across from Green-Wood Cemetery. The piece covered Daniel's fifteen years in coffee, the sneaker collection that gave the cafe its name, the Melbourne-roasted house blend, and the knitting group and running club the owners started to pull neighbors in.

Questions: How do two community farms bring fresh food to Sunset Park doorsteps?
Story Headline (If published): From Farm to Front Door: How Sunset Park Connects Through Fresh Food
Story Description or Prompt: Angela S. and Michal N. compared the two CSAs operating in Sunset Park: the volunteer-run Sunset Park CSA, founded in 2008 and serving nearly 100 households out of St. Michael's Church, and Harvest Share, a 2022 NYU Langone research project on a Brooklyn Grange rooftop near Industry City. Each writer described her own membership, and the piece laid out share prices, sliding scales, SNAP acceptance, and the culturally tailored Chinese and Mexican shares Harvest Share grows.

Questions: What is wage theft, and what can workers do about it?
Story Description or Prompt: An explainer from Documented, the nonprofit newsroom covering immigrant New York, defined wage theft and illustrated it with three cases: a busser whose manager pocketed cash tips, a renovation worker paid half his agreed rate, and a bakery cashier charged for uniform cleaning. It walked readers through looking up an employer on Documented's Wage Theft Monitor and listed the options for acting — a workers center, a labor lawyer, or a claim with the state Department of Labor.

Questions: What did 19 Sunset Park street vendors reveal about their lives in a one-day exhibit?
Story Headline (If published): ‘Venciendo el Miedo’ Puts Street Vendors in Focus
Story Description or Prompt: Carmen R. covered Venciendo el Miedo (Overcoming Fear), a one-day July 15 exhibit at Sunset Park Library presenting the photos, written narratives, and audio of 19 Sunset Park street vendors. The story traced the project to 14 weeks of photovoice workshops led by Voces Ciudadanas and advocacy director Valeria Paz Reyes, and named the four themes that emerged: fear, perseverance and survival, passing on traditions, and community building.

Questions: Can you name every crop in the Sunset Park Sun's cover illustration?
Story Description or Prompt: The back page ran a Crop Quiz built on Mattie Akers' cover illustration of CSA vegetables, asking readers to name each crop on a matching blank grid. Entries emailed by August 20 were eligible for the September issue, with five winners promised the vegetable or fruit of their choice at the next Library Newsroom session.

Questions: What does home mean in Sunset Park — and what threatens it?
Story Headline (If published): Home is where the rice balls are
Story Description or Prompt: Terry Parris Jr. opened the fourth issue on the theme of home in all its forms — the block you live on, the art on the streets, the community pool, and a plate of rice balls — and named affordability and the fear of losing a home as the pressure running underneath it. He framed the issue's stories as different answers to that: a café that became a gathering place, artists carving out room to work, neighbors sharing traditions, and a community wrestling with rent.

Questions: How did a family from Puebla turn a storefront on 61st Street into Sunset Park's living room?
Story Headline (If published): Gigi’s Coffee Shop Brews More Than Coffee in Sunset Park
Story Description or Prompt: Sol M. profiled GiGi's Coffee Shop at 511 61st Street, tracing Efren Dominguez and Guillermina Galicia's move from Puebla to Sunset Park in 2000 and Efren's climb from catering-hall dishwasher to head chef before the family opened the café in 2022. The piece covered the 2023 expansion into the space next door, the small library curated by daughter Bernice, and the birthday parties, quinceañeras, and Christmases that turned the shop into a gathering place; the interview was conducted in Spanish.

Questions: Where can artists in Sunset Park find affordable workspace?
Story Headline (If published): Where Can Artists in Sunset Park Work?
Story Description or Prompt: Susan P. opened a new feature on artist workspace by rounding up three places in Sunset Park where artists can make their work: the NARS Foundation at 201 46th Street, MADE Bush Terminal, and ArtBuilt at the Brooklyn Army Terminal. She described each one's residencies, studio leases, and workshops, noted the list was not exhaustive, and asked readers to write in with others or share their own workspace.

Questions: What is the fish-hunting raptor nesting at Bush Terminal Piers Park?
Story Headline (If published): Sunset Park Bird of the month: Osprey
Story Description or Prompt: Charlie DeWitt's Bird of the Month featured the osprey, a fish-eating water bird that nests on a platform at the lagoon bird sanctuary in Bush Terminal Piers Park, visible from the first pier off the 43rd Street entrance. The piece described the bird's white crest, brown cheek patch, 57-to-59-inch wingspan, and 80-mile-per-hour dives, and noted its comeback since the 1972 ban on DDT.

Questions: How much is rent going up for Sunset Park's stabilized tenants, and what can they do?
Story Headline (If published): Rent Guidelines Board Approves Increases: What Sunset Park Rent-Stabilized Tenants Should Know
Story Description or Prompt: Ahdya A. explained the Rent Guidelines Board's June 30, 2025 vote to raise rent-stabilized rents 3 percent on one-year leases and 4.5 percent on two-year leases, with worked examples on a $2,000 rent and instructions for checking whether an apartment qualifies. She set the increase against Sunset Park's numbers — roughly 1,000 buildings with stabilized units, about 63 percent renters, and 27.2 percent severely rent burdened in 2023 — and closed with what tenants can do, including getting help from Neighbors Helping Neighbors.

Questions: How are 54th Street neighbors raising $25,000 to replace the Unity Mural?
Story Headline (If published): 54th Street Comes Together to Paint a Picture
Story Description or Prompt: Adriana Alba covered the effort by 54th Street residents to replace the Sunset Park Unity Mural on the Citibank wall at 54th and 5th Avenue, which had not been updated since 2001. Block resident Katie Walsh assembled a task force of neighbors, Antonio M. canvassed the block for image ideas, and Brooklyn muralist Danielle Mastrion was selected; of the $25,000 needed, residents had raised $2,500 and the Sunset Park BID committed $10,000 under executive director David Estrada.

Questions: Thinking about buying a home? Where can you start in Sunset Park?
Story Description or Prompt: The team ran a short notice about free online Introduction to Homebuying workshops offered that fall by Neighbors Helping Neighbors, the HUD-certified housing counseling group based in Sunset Park. The sessions covered the basics of purchasing a first home and how housing counselors can help, with QR codes to register for the September 16 session in Spanish or the September 17 session in English.

Questions: How does a family recipe for rice balls travel from southern Italy to 48th Street?
Story Description or Prompt: Maureen C. shared Bernadette Wilson's arancini recipe, passed to her over 40 years ago by her sister-in-law's family from Basilicata in southern Italy and made for neighbors on 48th Street at the holidays. The page ran the full ingredient list, equipment, and four steps: cook the rice, mix in butter, egg yolks, grated cheese and mozzarella, bread the balls in egg white and breadcrumbs, and fry at 350°F.

Questions: What's moving through Sunset Park this month?
Story Description or Prompt: Terry Parris Jr. opened the fifth issue on the theme of motion — bikes threading through busy streets, festivals spilling onto avenues, students shaping paper and plaster into creatures, and the ongoing conversations about how the neighborhood builds and grows. He framed the issue's stories as different angles on that movement: delayed bike safety upgrades, a documentary screening, alebrijes for Día de los Muertos, the 5th Avenue Festival, and a bar that became a gathering place for art.

Questions: What does a decade-long documentary reveal about Industry City and Sunset Park?
Story Headline (If published): Screening of Emergent City at Sunset Park Library
Story Description or Prompt: The team previewed a free October 23 screening of Emergent City at the Sunset Park Library, the documentary filmed over more than a decade about the transformation of Industry City and what it meant for the neighborhood. The notice announced a post-screening conversation with co-director Jay Arthur Sterrenberg, gave the 5:30 p.m. start, and noted the event was supported by the Empire Wind Offshore Wind Project with RSVP by QR code.

Questions: How did a parade of more than 60 flags become Sunset Park's biggest street festival?
Story Headline (If published): Food, Flags, and Farm Animals: Sunset Park’s 5th Avenue Festival
Story Description or Prompt: Ciel J. P. traced the 26th anniversary of the Sunset Park BID 5th Avenue Festival back to its origins, from the 1994 Parade of Flags that drew more than 60 nations and even then-Mayor Giuliani, to the BID's first festival on October 23, 1999, with its sound stages, amusement rides, and farm animals. She described how the parade was eventually discontinued while its spirit carried into the September festival, now an unofficial celebration of the nine Latin American independence days that fall that month

Questions: What happened at the 26th annual Sunset Park BID Street Festival?
Story Headline (If published): Sunset Park BID Street Festival Recap
Story Description or Prompt: Michal N. recapped the 26th annual Sunset Park BID Street Festival on September 21, when thousands of neighbors filled fifteen blocks of 5th Avenue between 44th and 59th Streets for food, music, games, and a live animal display of parrots and snakes. She named the local businesses and elected officials with booths — among them State Senator Andrew Gounardes and Council Member Alexa Avilés — and noted the Sunset Park Sun's own table, where neighbors signed up for future issues.

Questions: What's Behind the Menu at Mama Tried?
Story Headline (If published): What’s Behind the Menu at...Mama Tried
Story Description or Prompt: Ray A. profiled Mama Tried, the bar at 3rd Avenue and 27th Street that Colin Strohm, Jessica Higgs, and Will Nolan opened in March 2021 under the BQE. The piece covered the backyard built with friends for live music, the drag karaoke and plant swaps, Will's food and cocktail menu including the New York Times–featured Pink Angel, and the wall of customers' mothers' photographs.

Questions: How can you help Sunset Park's street cats?
Story Headline (If published): How you can help sunset park's street cats
Story Description or Prompt: Edy R. wrote about the stray cats living in Sunset Park and the obstacles that shorten their lives, pointing readers to shelters and adoption groups including Animal Care Centers of NYC, Brooklyn Cat Cafe, and Angels for Mistreated Animals. She explained Trap Neuter Release as a humane method of population control and listed where to get training and spay-neuter help, from Neighborhood Cats to Flatbush Cats and the Brooklyn Bridge Animal Welfare Coalition.

Questions: What's standing in the way of safer biking in Sunset Park?
Story Headline (If published): Biking in Sunset Park Hits Bumps and Breakthroughs
Story Description or Prompt: Becca E. rounded up the state of cycling in Sunset Park, from the protected bike lane approved for 3rd Avenue between Prospect Avenue and 62nd Street — postponed by the Department of Transportation until at least 2026 after business groups objected — to the NYPD's switch to criminal summonses, which pushed citywide cyclist summonses from 561 to nearly 6,000 in a single quarter. She also covered the Citi Bike expansion into Bay Ridge, a planned dock at the 9th Avenue D stop, and the Oonee secure bike parking hub coming to the 25th Street R station.

Questions: How are Sunset Park High School students building mythical creatures for Día de los Muertos?
Story Headline (If published): Sunset Park High School Students Bring Mythical Creatures to Life for el Día de los Muertos at Green-Wood Cemetery
Story Description or Prompt: Anna Reid, a Sunset Park High School art teacher, described how her students were building large-scale plaster alebrijes for Green-Wood Cemetery's Día de los Muertos celebration, drawing on the legacy of Pedro Linares with designs inspired by water, earth, fire, and air. The piece recounted the school's past contributions of papel picado, cempasúchil, and ceramic alebrijes, and announced the November 1 unveiling at the Historic Chapel, where the community could help decorate a giant alebrije.

Questions: What has the Sunset Park Sun built in one year — and who built it?
Story Headline (If published): One Year Ago: We Sat Down for Lunch and Built Something Together
Story Description or Prompt: Terry Parris Jr. marked the Sunset Park Sun's first year by returning to the October 2024 Saturday lunch at Sunset Park Library, where about 20 strangers marked their most cherished spots on a map and the project took shape. He counted what followed — nearly two dozen sessions, almost 200 residents, more than 20 volunteers, and six issues carrying about three dozen stories — and pointed to Maureen and Carmen getting better at asking questions, Susan's first Community Board meeting, and Judith's answer on the recreation center as proof of what neighbors can do.

Questions: What can you say about Sunset Park in five lines and a ZIP code?
Story Description or Prompt: Diana M. introduced the ZipOde, a form created by the nonprofit O, Miami with the NPR-affiliated station WLRN in which each digit of a ZIP code sets the number of words in a line. She used 11220 to write eight short poems about Sunset Park, covering the Manhattan skyline seen from the park, Our Lady of Perpetual Help, Green-Wood Cemetery, the library, the neighborhood's closed stores, and the people who live here.

Questions: What's Behind the Menu at George's Restaurant?
Story Headline (If published): What's Behind the Menu at...George's Restaurant?
Story Description or Prompt: Carmen R. and Maureen C. profiled George's Restaurant at 5701 Fifth Avenue, opened in 1957 by Greek immigrant George Planzos II and run since 1987 by his son Teddy, who started there at 15. The piece traced three generations of the family in the restaurant trade, the expansions into a former pharmacy and barbershop, and the menu's shift toward Dominican mangu and Mexican carne asada as the neighborhood's Irish and Scandinavian customers gave way to Latino and Chinese ones.

Questions: What is the year-round city bird you see at the waterfront and Green-Wood?
Story Headline (If published): Sunset Park Sun Bird of the Month: Canada Goose
Story Description or Prompt: Charlie DeWitt's Bird of the Month featured the Canada goose, or Branta canadensis, a year-round city resident he watches at the waterfront park and Green-Wood Cemetery. The piece covered the bird's markings and 43-to-60-inch wingspan, its bowl-shaped nests and lifelong pairings, and the 2009 euthanizing of city geese after the LaGuardia bird strike, which many birders called both controversial and ineffective.

Questions: Where does Sunset Park begin and end, and what do three different maps get wrong? (中文版)
Story Description or Prompt: Michal N.'s boundaries story, first published in English in the August 2025 issue, ran here in Chinese translation, comparing how Google Maps, the New York Times' 2023 crowd-sourced neighborhood map, and Community Board 7 each draw Sunset Park's edges and finding that no two matched. It also collected building names pointing somewhere else — Park Slope Homes, two Linden Heights sites, Sunset Ridge Cafe & Grill, the former Bay Ridge Savings Bank, and a Greenwood Heights Reformed Church property marker — and asked who gets to decide what a neighborhood is called.

Questions: Where does Sunset Park begin and end, and what borrowed names are hiding in plain sight? (Versión en español)
Story Description or Prompt: Michal N.'s boundaries story, first published in English in the August 2025 issue, ran here in Spanish translation, setting Google Maps, the New York Times' 2023 crowd-sourced neighborhood map, and Community Board 7 against each other and finding no two drew the same Sunset Park. It carried the same set of misplaced building names — Park Slope Homes, Linden Heights, Sunset Ridge Cafe & Grill, the old Bay Ridge Savings Bank, and the Greenwood Heights Reformed Church marker — and closed by asking readers for strange or borrowed names they had noticed.

Questions: Need help starting a business? What can Sunset Park Library do for you?
Story Description or Prompt: The team ran a notice that Sunset Park Library was hosting free one-on-one support for entrepreneurs every Wednesday from 10 a.m. to noon and 2 to 4 p.m., and every Friday from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. It listed what librarians could help with — registering a business, accessing loans or grants, permits, marketing, finances, and small-business tech tools — and noted that no appointment or RSVP was necessary.

Questions: What legal basics should a new business owner know?
Story Description or Prompt: The team announced a free legal basics class for start-ups at Sunset Park Library on November 13 at 5:30 p.m., presented by The Legal Aid Society's Community Development Project. The training introduced the different business entities — sole proprietorships, partnerships, LLCs, and corporations — and what each means for liability and taxes, with no RSVP needed in person and a QR code for joining by Zoom with Spanish interpretation.

Questions: Can you write a poem about Sunset Park using your ZIP code?
Story Description or Prompt: The back page invited readers to write their own ZipOde after Diana M.'s poems, explaining that each digit of a ZIP code sets the words in that line and that a 0 lets the writer choose anything from one to nine. It suggested writing about a block, a favorite view, or the neighbors, left ruled space to fill in, and asked readers to drop poems at the Sunset Park Library or photograph the page and email it in.

Questions: What is the gift at the heart of the Sunset Park Sun?
Story Headline (If published): The Gift of Curiosity, Connection, and Community
Story Description or Prompt: Terry Parris Jr. opened the December issue on the idea of the gift, naming the work neighbors do together — sitting at a library table helping someone think through a story, hearing a sharper question than last month, watching a volunteer walk in with a head full of ideas — as the gift at the center of it. He described the bulletin as wrapping paper around the neighborhood itself, promised more sessions, stories, and experiments in 2026, and invited readers to send ideas and questions.

Questions: Who won in Sunset Park on November 4, and what does the new city government look like?
Story Headline (If published): Mamdani Makes History; Aviles Wins Sunset Park
Story Description or Prompt: The Sunset Park Sun team recapped the November 4, 2025 citywide election, in which Zohran Mamdani won the mayoralty with just over 50 percent of the vote against Andrew Cuomo's 42 percent and Curtis Sliwa's 7 percent, and took 60 percent in Sunset Park. The piece noted Mamdani would be the city's first Muslim and first South Asian mayor and the youngest in more than a century, reported Council Member Alexa Avilés holding District 38 with nearly 73 percent, and listed the other citywide results and all six ballot proposals.

Questions: Who's behind the holiday display that's lit up 50th Street for 25 years?
Story Description or Prompt: Edy R. wrote about the holiday display at 469 50th Street that she had admired for more than 20 years, and about meeting Hector and Noraima, the couple behind it, who have lived in Sunset Park for 31 years and decorated for 25 consecutive ones. The piece covered the three weeks of solo work Hector puts in each year starting before Thanksgiving, the family member who appears as Santa when his schedule allows, and the single instance of vandalism in all that time.

Questions: How do the holiday lights come back to 5th Avenue every year?
Story Headline (If published): Sunset Park's Holiday Lights and Tree Lighting Return to 5th Avenue
Story Description or Prompt: Cinthya O. covered the return of the holiday lights between 38th and 64th Streets, a tradition begun by the Fifth Avenue Merchants Association and carried by the Sunset Park BID for more than 30 years, with the 64th Street festoon missing that year because of bridge construction. She reported the more than $40,000 cost and DOT permitting from BID executive director David Estrada, and previewed the 23rd annual tree lighting on December 5 at 5th Avenue and 60th Street, with 500 goodie bags, a Santa trolley, and support from OLPH, the Clarimar Group, Anthem Blue Cross/Blue Shield, and the NYPD.

Questions: Need a last-minute gift? Which Sunset Park shops have you covered?
Story Headline (If published): Last-Minute Gifts? Sunset Park has you covered
Story Description or Prompt: Ciel J. P. built a last-minute gift guide out of six neighborhood small businesses, noting there are more than 600 businesses on 5th Avenue alone. The list covered Mr. C's Cycles, Blossom Flower Shop, Hong Fu Baby, Zapateria Mexico, Daysun Restaurant Supplies, and ValuPlus Thrift Shop with addresses and what to buy at each, and asked readers to send in shops for future guides.

Questions: What goes into Sunset Park's award-winning coquito?
Story Description or Prompt: Carmen R. explained coquito, the coconut drink at the center of Puerto Rican Christmas, and profiled longtime Sunset Park resident Cynthia Gonzalez, who built her own recipe by tasting as she went and won the Brooklyn Coquito Masters contest with it in 2016. The page ran Gonzalez's full ingredient list, equipment, and six steps, and noted the December 6 Brooklyn qualifying competition at Uprose.

Questions: Where can you snack for under $10 in Sunset Park?
Story Headline (If published): Snacking on a Budget: Sunset Park Snacks We Found for Under $10
Story Description or Prompt: The Sunset Park Sun team assembled a guide to neighborhood snacks under $10, leading with four picks — La Isla's $3 alcapurrias, El Guayaquileño's $6 morocho, L'wren Bar's $8 happy hour plates, and Key Food's store-made pico de gallo — with background on the Puerto Rican and Ecuadorian dishes behind two of them. A second page listed a dozen more spots by avenue, from Huahui Bakery to Ba Xuyên and Kai Feng Fu Dumpling, alongside a custom Google map, and asked readers what was missing.

Questions: What is the soft-voiced swan gliding through Brooklyn's parks and cemeteries?
Story Headline (If published): Sunset Park Sun Bird of the Month: The Mute Swan
Story Description or Prompt: Charlie DeWitt's Bird of the Month featured the mute swan, which despite its name calls softly to other swans and to its cygnets, and which spread from Europe into ponds and lakes across all five boroughs. The piece covered the birds' lifelong pairings and big black paddle-shaped feet, and pointed readers to the Brooklyn Bird Club's Saturday morning walks at the Prospect Park Boathouse and to Green-Wood Cemetery and Bush Terminal Piers Park as places to look.

Questions: Where can you find free food in Sunset Park this holiday season?
Story Headline (If published): Sunset Park Food Pantries and Hot Meals Guide
Story Description or Prompt: The Sun ran a directory of food pantries, hot meal programs, and mobile markets serving Sunset Park, compiled for the holiday season by the office of Council Member Alexa Avilés.
